title: Spring syrup feeding for honey bee colonies
subtitle: Early spring feed stimulates brood rearing. Give it too early and it ferments; too late and the colony misses the buildup window.
excerpt: A thin sugar syrup fed in early spring stimulates a colony that has depleted its winter stores. The bees interpret the incoming syrup as a nectar flow and increase egg-laying to match. The right timing is when daytime temperatures are reliably above 10°C and bees are flying on warm afternoons. Feed too cold and the syrup sits uneaten or ferments.
sourceNotes: NBU Beekeeper's Toolkit (2024), feeding section. BBKA Bee Craft technical notes on spring management. Frank Pearson, Bee-keeping for All (1923), Internet Archive, chapter on spring stimulation. NBU advisory on fondant vs syrup feeding timing.

glossaryTerms.definition: The proportion of sugar to water in a sugar syrup. A 1:1 syrup (equal parts by weight) is thin, used for spring stimulation. A 2:1 syrup is thick, used for autumn winter preparation and store building.
When bees from another colony enter a hive to steal syrup or honey stores. Triggered by open food sources or a hive entrance too wide to defend when the colony is weak.

content.text: Spring syrup at a 1:1 ratio (1 kg sugar dissolved in 1 litre warm water) tells the colony that a nectar flow has started. The queen responds by increasing her laying rate and the colony expands faster than it would on reserves alone. The window is from late February or March in a warm year through to early April, while the colony is still compact and the first natural forage, willow, hazel, blackthorn, is opening.

Use white granulated sugar only. Brown sugar and unrefined sugars contain minerals and trace compounds that bees cannot process safely. Dissolve the sugar in hot (not boiling) water, stirring until clear. Allow to cool to room temperature before filling the feeder. A syrup added hot to a feeder sitting on a cool hive will condense on the colony below, chilling the bees nearest the feeder.
Spring is a time of nectar scarcity. Any open sugar source will attract foragers from surrounding colonies. Prevent
by feeding in the early evening, reducing hive entrance to one bee-width if using an entrance reducer, and not spilling syrup near the entrance.
Place a contact or top-mounted feeder directly over the cluster, not at the side of the hive. Bees in a cool spring cannot travel across a cold gap to reach feed.

Fill the feeder with 500 ml-1 litre at a time. A colony returning syrup to stores fast enough to need daily top-ups is a strong colony; a colony that has left the feeder untouched for three days in mild weather has a problem worth investigating.

Remove the feeder once natural forage is well underway. This is usually when oil-seed rape or fruit blossom is fully open. A colony still being fed when a strong nectar flow arrives will fill supers with syrup, not honey.

After 2-3 weeks of spring feeding, a colony building well will have increased in warmth when you lift the roof, more bees visible around the entrance on sunny afternoons, and a noticeably larger brood area on inspection. A colony not responding to stimulative feeding at this stage needs a full inspection to check for a laying queen and adequate brood space. The
